Out of Spec: Satellites, Tarantulas, and Frontier Calibration

A working game concept, vocabulary guide, and four-week vertical slice roadmap for a chunky 3D voxel life-sim blending off-world remote farming, indoor arachnid husbandry, and satirical metrology.

The elevator pitch you can hand to anyone

The fastest way to stop feeling stuck at the start of a game project is to lock down a single, vivid sentence that explains what the player actually does. Right now, your concept is not "Stardew Valley in space." It is a precision-and-drift frontier life-sim where you are the lone certified metrology contractor on a half-baked corporate colony, juggling an automated outdoor farm you steer through a handheld satellite phone and an indoor conservatory of rare tarantulas whose bio-silk keeps your instruments in tolerance.

Start by building a playable four-week vertical slice in Godot 4 rather than writing lore or designing fifty crops. One voxel field, one remote tractor with signal lag, one terrarium with a drifting humidity sensor, and one absurd corporate audit drop-pod will prove the entire game faster than a hundred pages of notes.

“Graveyard Keeper’s cynical corporate humor meets Stardew Valley’s daily rhythm—except your watering can is a Starlink-linked rover that drifts out of spec.”

Working title: Out of Spec (placeholder—easy to swap once your colony name and MegaCorp parody click).

Target feel: Tactile, slightly absurd, deeply satisfying when every sensor hits green.

How to describe your visual and tonal direction

When you prompt AI art tools, write design notes, or explain your idea to friends, vague words like "futuristic" or "voxel" produce generic results. Use these three concrete pillars as your shared vocabulary across every prompt and prototype.

Chunky diorama voxels

Think MagicaVoxel or Touryst-style lighting rather than flat Minecraft blocks. Keep character and rover silhouettes chunky and readable from a three-quarter isometric camera, with crisp global illumination so glowing amber heat lamps and cyan satellite beams pop against dark alien rock.

Corporate frontier satire

Borrow Graveyard Keeper’s dry, bureaucratic comedy. Orbiting MegaCorp cares obsessively about ISO-style compliance stickers, calibration certificates, and quarterly telemetry quotas—even while the colony’s power grid flickers and alien weeds chew through the fiber lines.

Analog-meets-orbital UI

Your in-game handheld phone is the star interface. Give it chunky tactile switches, signal-strength bars, tolerance bands, and cheerful passive-aggressive notifications from orbital dispatch, making remote farming feel completely distinct from swinging a hoe by hand.

Two distinct pillars that feed each other

Having two contrasting spaces—a warm, quiet indoor sanctuary and a sprawling, hazard-prone outdoor frontier—gives your daily routine natural pacing. Neither pillar feels like a disconnected minigame because each one supplies the exact resource the other needs to scale.

Indoors: The Tarantula Conservatory

Your dome is your cozy sanctuary. You collect, house, and breed both grounded real-world inspired species and bizarre off-world morphs. Each enclosure relies on calibrated micro-climate sensors (temperature, humidity, substrate vibration) that gradually drift.

  • Cozy care loop: Mist enclosures, monitor pre-molt stages, upgrade voxel terrarium decor, and unlock rare color morphs.
  • Precision output: Healthy, stress-free tarantulas shed ultra-uniform optical silk, micro-filaments, and bioactive compounds used to craft tighter reference standards and high-tier satellite transceivers.

Outdoors: Satellite-Linked Farm and Mine

Instead of walking across forty tiles with a watering can, you pull out your handheld field phone and uplink to orbital relays to pilot chunky voxel tractors, mowers, and crystal-mining drills across terraced alien terrain.

  • Hybrid control curve: Early on, you drive one scrappy rover manually over a laggy link while dodging signal dead zones. As you level up, you place voxel relay towers, record path routines, and manage an entire fleet from a tactical map.
  • Resource return: Harvested frontier crops, alien moss substrates, and crystalline ores supply your colony town, fund corporate fees, and build advanced terrarium habitats back indoors.

Turning metrology and calibration into playful progression

Real calibration is about trust, drift, and guardbanding—and those exact ideas translate naturally into hilarious, rewarding game mechanics when you introduce them in three layers rather than dumping everything on the player on Day 1.

Progression Tier Metrology Mechanic What Happens When Out of Spec Player Reward for Tightening Tolerance
Early Game (Days 1–10) Drift & Tolerance Tuning
Quick tactile zeroing of rover steering, mower cut-height, and terrarium hygrometers.		 Tractor veers diagonally through prized crops; mower shaves boulders; heat lamp turns a humid enclosure into a sauna. Clean harvest yields, happy molting tarantulas, and longer intervals before recalibration is needed.
Mid Game (Days 11–30) Corporate Audits & Contracts
Rotating orbital inspection orders, mystery alien gauges, and satirical compliance forms.		 MegaCorp slaps your outpost with petty fines, locks out premium drop-pods, or sends a passive-aggressive auditor drone. Higher clearance tiers, black-market calibration work from colonists, and legal permits for deeper mining canyons.
Late Game (Day 31+) Precision Crafting & Signal Alignment
Aligning multi-dish relay arrays and using tarantula optical silk to build sub-micron standards.		 Solar flares scramble autopilot routes; high-grade ores shatter into low-value dust during uncalibrated drilling. Full fleet autopilot across the entire plateau, legendary alien arachnid morphs, and top-grade orbital exports.

Why every single day feels different

Stardew Valley and Graveyard Keeper stay addictive because no two mornings share the exact same priorities. Combining a small walkable colony town with handheld comms and orbital drop-pods gives you three overlapping calendars that constantly remix your to-do list.

Orbital weather and signal windows

Clear days give crisp low-latency satellite links for big mining pushes. Ion storms and solar flares create dead zones—pushing you to spend the day indoors tending molting tarantulas, running bench calibrations, or visiting town.

Drop-pod dispatches and audits

Your phone buzzes each morning with rotating contracts: a rush calibration on a colonist’s broken moisture probe, a surprise MegaCorp compliance check on Day 5, or a shady orbital trader dropping rare tarantula slings for twelve hours only.

Quirky colony neighbors

A tight cast of six to eight eccentric colonists—a rival calibration contractor who cuts corners, a botanist terrified of spiders until she sees your silk quality, a scrapyard rover mechanic—gives you personal errands, banter, and town upgrades without bloating your writing scope.

Picking the right engine for an AI-assisted solo build

Because you already have Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok subscriptions—and strong TypeScript and systems instincts—your biggest risk is not coding difficulty; it is picking an engine with heavy boilerplate or slow iteration. Godot 4 is the strongest overall choice for a shippable Steam/PC voxel game, with Three.js / React Three Fiber as an optional 48-hour web sandbox if you want to test rover controls in a browser first.

Engine / Stack Voxel Asset Pipeline AI Code-Gen Fit Steam / PC Readiness Verdict for This Game
Godot 4 (GDScript) Seamless MagicaVoxel .gltf import plus native GridMap terrain Excellent—concise scripts, readable scene files, zero boilerplate Native Windows, Mac, Linux exports; lightweight and royalty-free Primary Pick: Best balance of speed, 3D lighting, and indie shipping power.
Three.js / R3F (TypeScript) Clean .glb loading, fast UI overlay in React/Tailwind Outstanding—LLMs excel at TypeScript and React UI (great for the phone UI) Web-first; requires Electron/Tauri wrapper for Steam Fast Sandbox: Ideal if you want a playable browser test in one weekend.
Unity (C#) Huge voxel asset store and mature shader tools Very strong C# generation, though heavier editor setup Industry-standard PC and console pipeline Solid alternative only if you already prefer C# and want prebuilt store packs.

Asset shortcut: Pair Godot 4 with MagicaVoxel (free, fast, and iconic for chunky 3D voxels). You can model a tractor, a terrarium, and a satellite dish in an evening, export straight to .gltf, and drop them into Godot with glowing emission materials.

Your four-week vertical slice: where to start tomorrow

Never start an indie life-sim by building the full map, skill tree, and town. Start with a Vertical Slice—one five-minute playable day that proves the core fantasy is fun. Once those five minutes feel great, adding more crops, tarantula species, and NPCs is pure joy.

  1. Week 1 — Build the "Greybox" Rover & Phone Screen: Drop a flat voxel plot and one placeholder cube-tractor into Godot 4. Wire up an on-screen handheld phone overlay that steers the tractor, tills soil blocks, and introduces noticeable input lag when you drive behind a rock out of satellite line-of-sight.
  2. Week 2 — Add One Tarantula Terrarium & One Drift Mechanic: Create a single indoor glass enclosure with a temperature/humidity readout that slowly wanders out of spec. When you recalibrate it at your bench, the tarantula molts and drops one spool of optical silk—which you slot into your dish to cut rover lag in half.
  3. Week 3 — Wire the Day Clock & Satirical Drop-Pod: Add a morning-to-night cycle, a daily phone dispatch from MegaCorp ("Your tractor wheel circumference is 1.4% non-compliant"), and a physical drop-pod that lands outside to collect crops or drop fines.
  4. Week 4 — Replace Greyboxes with MagicaVoxel Models & Add One Colonist: Swap your placeholder cubes for three chunky MagicaVoxel assets (tractor, dome, terrarium), add warm amber vs. cyan lighting, and drop in one quirky neighbor who trades you a rover upgrade. Playtest it yourself—if those five minutes feel fun, you have a real game.

“Split your AI subscriptions by specialty: one for architecture, one for rapid code, one for satire, and one for visual references.”

Use Claude for clean GDScript/TypeScript architecture and refactoring, Gemini for visual concept boards, design docs, and broad worldbuilding synthesis, ChatGPT for structured data tables (crop growth curves, drift math, tarantula species JSON), and Grok for punchy, irreverent corporate satire and weird NPC dialogue drafts.
